extracted.intended_audience: elementary school teachers and young-writer instructors (and students learning craft)
extracted.subtask_description: A mini-lesson and author study focused on teaching elementary-level writers how to write from a character's perspective, using Beverly Cleary's techniques (concrete language, humor, small words, homonyms) with classroom activities and examples. Includes objectives, examples, discussion prompts, and facilitation guidance for classroom use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing from the perspective of a character
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors write from the perspective of a character when they use first-person and deep-third point(s) of view to show story events from the body, the mind, and the heart of the character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This craft helps the reader see and experience events as the character does rather than simply watching; Cleary chose Leigh's voice in Dear Mr. Henshaw to express real emotions after parental separation. Use mentor-text examples (Dear Mr. Henshaw, Ramona Quimby, Number the Stars) and have students write short stories from a chosen character's perspective. Classroom implementation: present examples, ask students to recall instances, then have them write and share with partners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete language for concrete physical humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Use specific, concrete sensory details to create physical/comedic moments that elementary readers can easily understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Ramona Quimby, Age 8: 'She took a firm hold on her egg, waited until everyone at her table was watching, and whack—she found herself with a hand full of crumbled shell and something cool and slimy running down her face.' Concrete language makes humor accessible to young readers. Teaching tip: model concrete descriptions and encourage students to write similarly vivid physical actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing with humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally craft humorous scenes or characterization to engage readers, noting that humor is difficult and not every writer does it comfortably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a student finds humor challenging, using concrete language and specific physical comedy can help. Provide examples and model your own comedic scenes (teacher shares) and encourage practice. The author notes humor 'is not easy and I don’t think everyone is capable of doing it effectively and comfortably.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Using small words to say big things
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor simple, small words that nevertheless convey strong meaning and clear characterization instead of large, complex vocabulary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleary often uses small words to reveal character quickly (examples: 'big show-off', 'tattletale'). Teaching suggestion: encourage substitutes like 'fishy' for 'suspicious' or 'snoopy' for 'inquisitive' to maintain accessibility and voice for young readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using homonyms to teach vocabulary and layered meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ homonyms (words with multiple meanings) in context to teach vocabulary and create moments of misunderstanding or double-meaning that are instructive and entertaining.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from Ramona the Pest: teacher saying 'Sit here for the present' leads Ramona to think of a gift. Classroom application: have students create sentences that exploit homonyms (teacher suggests using 'fly' with two senses: bird movement vs. insect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express real emotions without being overemotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Show characters' genuine feelings and inner life while avoiding melodrama or overemphasis; let the character's voice convey emotion naturally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cleary 'has chosen to write from the perspective of the character Leigh to express the real emotions that many children experience, but she does it in a way that is not overemotional.' Teach balance by analyzing passages that show emotion through detail and voice rather than expository statements of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mentor texts and examples to teach craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce and analyze short examples from established authors (Cleary and others) and the teacher's own writing to demonstrate techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lesson plan: present a PowerPoint with learning objectives, examples of Cleary's writing, when/why to use the craft, and additional examples. Ask students to recall examples from readings. Modeling by the teacher encourages student participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning objectives: understand and apply the craft
rubrics_metrics.description: Set clear, assessable learning objectives: (1) students will understand Beverly Cleary’s craft of writing from the perspective of characters; (2) students will be able to use the technique themselves in their writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the objectives to guide activities and assessment: have students draft stories using character perspective, share with partners, and submit work for teacher feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classroom activity structure: pair writing, peer feedback, and teacher facilitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure student practice by having students write short stories from a character's perspective, share with a partner, provide peer feedback, and submit writing for teacher review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitation tips: teacher models first, circulates while pairs work, prompts hesitant groups, answers vocabulary or structure questions, and collects papers at the end for teacher feedback. Use discussion prompts ('How can you make the readers live the experience?', 'In what way will you use the technique?') to focus student reflection.
